title: Catch That Kid
full_review:
A young girl and her two friends decide to rob a high-security bank in order to pay for her dad's costly life-saving operation in the cleverly conceived but morally askew kiddie caper, "Catch That Kid" (20th Century Fox). Despite a smart script and a fresh-faced cast that gives the flick's shopworn heist plot a youthful twist, director Bart Freundlich uses an end-justifies-the-means attitude to rationalize his improbable premise, making it difficult to wholeheartedly applaud an otherwise entertaining family-friendly action movie.

Based on a Danish import, "Klatretosen" (2001), "Catch That Kid" stars Kristen Stewart as Maddy, a precocious 12-year-old whose father (Sam Robards), an ex-mountaineer and now go-cart track proprietor, finds himself paralyzed in a hospital bed due to a spinal injury incurred during an earlier near-fatal climbing accident. The only hope offered by doctors is an experimental overseas procedure with a hefty price tag well beyond the financial reach of Maddy's mom (Jennifer Beals), a security specialist currently installing an impregnable vault and surveillance system in a fortress-like bank, whose reptilian president (Michael Des Barres) callously denies her a loan request.

Blessed with her father's gene for scaling heights and entree to her mother's laptop full of access codes, Kristen secretly masterminds a plot to break into the bank and steal the $250,000 for her father's surgery. Aiding and abetting are her two best friends, rival suitors Gus (Max Thieriot), a go-cart grease monkey serving as the crew's wheelman, and Austin (Corbin Bleu), a budding Spielberg and computer whiz brought on board to hack into the bank's mainframe.

In addition to figuring out how to reach the state-of-the-art safe, which is suspended a hundred feet above the floor of the vault, the trio also has to deal with a bumblingly sadistic security guard (James Le Gros) and a patrolling pack of vicious Rottweilers. Like most heist films, much of the action involves the planning and execution of the elaborate scheme -- but then again, most cat burglars don't have to worry about being grounded or taking their 2-year-old brother along for the job because their mom couldn't find a baby sitter.

Unlike the young protagonists in the "Spy Kids" franchise who rely heavily on an array of high-tech gadgets, Kristen's prepubescent posse is just normal kids in a desperate situation using skills many adolescents are good at in real life (rock climbing, go-cart racing, etc.) to accomplish their goal, making their action-packed mini-"Mission-Impossible" all the more enjoyable, if not quite believable.

While the seen-it-a-hundred-times-before heist sequences are surprisingly entertaining, it is the young cast members themselves who, er, steal the show. Stewart radiates a ripening maturity beyond her years and Thieriot and Bleu effectively capture the vernal elan of puppy love when one kiss is worth being sent up the river -- or at least to your room.

On a troubling note, "Catch That Kid," like the recent "The Perfect Score," treats the characters' criminal actions with laissez-faire flippancy, as if to say lying, stealing and manipulating people's emotions are viable solutions to life's problems. While the film's lighthearted tone keeps these erroneous ethics somewhat in check, its hip, child-friendly coating makes the story's it's-OK-to-do-a-bad-thing-as-long-as-it's-for-a-noble-cause sentiment an easier pill for kids to swallow. Of course, to a 12-year-old with a father in the hospital this misguided logic may make perfect sense. But Freundlich is not 12 and he should understand that his film, which ultimately condemns the very actions it spent the previous 90-plus minutes making seem so cool, could be misleading to young viewers: "Gee, Mom, can Santa bring me a go-cart next Christmas so I can be chased by the police, too?"

Unfortunately, such a mixed-bag message might make this one movie some parents may not want their kids to catch.

Due to an ambiguous attitude toward larceny, minimal mildly crude humor and some action violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
